Testimony of Lt. Bruce Scott
AGAINST LD 1508

An Act to Clarify the Law Regarding Tinted Windows in Motor
Vehicles
Senator Nangle, Rep. Crafts, and distinguished Members of the Ioint
Standing Committee on Transportation, my name is Lt. Bruce Scott, and I am the Commanding Qfficer of the State Police Traffic Safety Unit. I am here today to testify on behalf of the Deparnnent of Public
Safety and the Maine State Police in Opposition to LD 1508.

This bill, if passed, would compel the Chief of the State Police to issue
medical tint waivers for vehicles to those that have submitted a proper
application, even when it is not in the best interest of public safety, or
in violation of federal law or not for purposes intended by the exception. Current law has a process in place that allows the State
Police to issue a medical waiver to a person who usually occupies the
vehicle if they are adversely affected by sunlight. The State Police has seen an increase in these medical window tint waiver applications over the years from 35 in 2.014 to 2.88 in 2.024 and we-expect these numbers
to continue to grow.

Our agency recognizes the importance in protecting everyone from the
harmful UV rays emitted by the sun and can appreciate the use of
window tint for those with light sensitivities. Like many well-
intentioned laws intended to protect those in certain situations with certain conditions, this exemption has already turned into a free for all
to anyone that has a medical care provider that is willing to sign a waiver for any purpose. This bill would take away the discretion of the
State Police to limit abuse, prevent multiple waivers for multiple
vehicles to the same person and would allow for tint to applied to
windshields, which is currently not allowed.

The law already allows a person to apply unlimited window tint on a windshield above the AS1 line, window tint on driver and passenger side Windows as long at least 35% light can be transmitted through them and unlimited tint to all rear windows behind the B--post and
rear windshield. This is allowed without a medical waiver and even though 1oo% lawful, makes it difficult for an operator to see clearly in low light conditions. The current medical waiver additionally allows a vehicle to have unlimited window tint on the driver and passenger windows, but this bill would allow the unlimited tinting on windshields as well. The Window tinting of windshields should never be allowed as the danger to public safety is greatly outweighed by the
very limited any) medical benefit.
Those with light sensitivity issues have reported a great improvement
following these current laws and can wear sunglasses when the sun is
too bright coming through the windshield. The windshield already
blocks from 94% to 99% of the harmful rays of the sun because they
are constructed with laminated glass, which consists of two layers of glass bonded together with a plastic interlayer. Also, you can purchase
UV blocking film that doesn't have any tint to it if someone needs
additional protection. To my knowledge, when this law went into
effect the only window film that blocked UV rays was tinted, hence the
medical need for tint waivers. With modern advances in solar
protection, there really isn't a medical need at all to have tinted
windows.

In the recent past we have had a couple different medical providers
call our office to inquire about what conditions qualified a person to

Testimony of Representative Dan Shagoury introducing
LD 1508, An Act to Clarify the Law Regarding Tinted Windows in
Motor Vehicles
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation

Good aftemoon, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation. I am Representative Dan Shagoury, and I represent House District
55 - the communities of Hallowell, Manchester and West Gardiner. I am pleased to present LD 1508, An Act to Clarify the Law Regarding Tinted Windows in Motor Vehicles.

You probably hear this a lot, I know we do in our committee, but this really is a very simple bill.
A constituent of mine, who owns a tinting shop, came to me with the idea for this bill. She said
that there had been issues with the police for some of her customers who, even though they had
valid medical exemptions, were told they could not have the protective film on their windows.
In an attempt to prevent this sort of misunderstanding, I changed "may" in the exemption
language to "shall." Additionally, the bill clarifies and specifies exactly which providers could provide the exemption. That's it.

What it doesn't do is change anything else concerning levels of tint and areas that can be tinted without an exemption from a medical provider. The exemption will still have to go to the police to be validated. And the police can still stop a person who they suspect of having illegally
darkened auto glass. But if the driver has an approval based on medical necessity, which they should always have with them, then they can go on their way.
I have heard that the State Police will be opposing this bill, and I'm a little disappointed. They
foresee lots of people getting these exemptions, and I suppose, by extension, lots of medical
providers giving them out unnecessarily. I don't see that happening. What I see happening is that the relatively few people with valid medical reasons for needing the window treatments will have more protection.

Thank you very much for your consideration. My constituent will be following me, and she has
the expertise about the window treatment process, but I will be glad to attempt to answer any
questions.

District 55: Hallowell, Manchester and West Gardiner
